card.name: Morris Dance
card.tagline: England's bell-jingling village ritual dance — handkerchiefs, sticks, white clothes, blackened faces, bells at the knees; the spring fertility tradition that refuses to die.
card.profile: Morris dance is the centuries-old ritual folk dance of the English villages — earliest written records date to the 15th century — performed by costumed troupes (sides) wearing white shirts and trousers with bells strapped to their shins. Dancers move in formation around a leader, sometimes carrying handkerchiefs to wave, sometimes striking wooden sticks together in synchronized patterns. Multiple regional traditions survive: Cotswold morris (the most familiar), Border morris (darker, more theatrical), Long Sword and Rapper morris (with metal swords), and the women's Northwest morris from Lancashire. Morris is performed each May 1st (May Day) by surviving sides across England.
card.insight: Morris dancing has been performed continuously in some English villages for over 500 years — the Bampton Morris in Oxfordshire claims an unbroken tradition since the 1500s, danced every Whit Monday since records began. The English Folk Dance and Song Society (founded by Cecil Sharp in 1911) saved morris from extinction in the early 20th century by documenting every surviving village tradition; today around 800 morris sides perform across England, the United States, and Australia.
